name: Implicit stereotype
statement: Knowing what a stereotype says and endorsing it are separable, and the association can fire on a cue and shape a later judgement in people who reject the content.
meaning: An implicit stereotype is an association between a social category and a trait, inferred from what a cue does to the speed or the content of a judgement that follows. Three claims travel under the one name and they are not equally supported. The first is that such associations exist and can be activated without the perceiver intending it. The second is that activation follows from categorisation alone, in everyone, whatever the person believes. The third is that these associations cause the discrimination that field experiments measure in hiring and housing. Evidence for the first is good within limits, for the second poor, and for the third indirect. Two neighbouring questions have their own entries and are not answered here. Whether the Implicit Association Test measures a stable trait, and what its scores predict, belongs to the entry on that test, which also covers the attempts to train scores down. The shooter task and its replication record belong to the entry on shooter bias.

origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Three studies built on a dissociation between automatic and controlled processes. Devine's claim was that high- and low-prejudice people know the same cultural stereotype, that the stereotype activates for both, and that rejecting it takes deliberate effort.

evidence: Devine's Study 1 asked 40 white introductory psychology students to list the content of the cultural stereotype of Black people regardless of their own beliefs. The seven-item Modern Racism Scale, with Cronbach's alpha of .83, split them by median into 21 high-prejudice and 19 low-prejudice subjects. Sixteen coding categories were used, and two judges agreed on 88% of classifications. None of the differences between the two groups was statistically reliable, and two further judges could not sort the protocols by prejudice level. Study 2 screened 483 students and ran 78 white subjects in the judgement condition. Words were flashed outside the fixation point for 80 ms and masked, 100 trials in all, with either 80% or 20% of them related to the racial stereotype and none denoting hostility. The primes carried the category and its content together: Blacks, Negroes and nigger sat alongside lazy, welfare and ghetto. Subjects then read a paragraph about an ambiguously hostile man named Donald and rated him on twelve scales. Hostility-related ratings ran to 7.52 in the 80% condition against 6.87 in the 20% condition, a priming by scale interaction of F(1, 70) = 5.04, p < .03. The six scales unrelated to hostility gave 5.89 in the 20% condition and 6.00 in the 80%, and prejudice level did not qualify the effect, F(1, 70) = 1.19, p = .27. Of 1,200 guesses in the awareness check, 20 were correct, a hit rate of 1.67%. Study 3 gave 67 students an anonymous thought-listing task about Black Americans. Sixty percent of the high-prejudice subjects wrote hostility themes and 9% of the low-prejudice subjects did, z = 4.41, p < .01. Banaji and Hardin made the same point about gender with reaction times. Sixty-eight Yale students saw one of 150 primes for 200 ms, then a blank screen for 100 ms, then a pronoun to be judged male or female. Judgements were faster when prime and target matched in gender, F(1, 66) = 117.56, p < .0001, with Cohen's d of .78 for primes gendered by definition and .47 for primes gendered by normative base rates. Thirty-seven of the 68 were aware of the prime-target relation, and aware and unaware subjects produced the same pattern, all Fs < 1. Three explicit measures of gender belief correlated with the priming score at -.003, -.050 and .037, none of them reliable. Their Experiment 2 matters more than their first, because it swapped the gender judgement for a pronoun versus non-pronoun judgement and so removed the overlap between prime and response. The congruency effect survived there at F(1, 56) = 4.63, p < .04. It held for primes gendered by definition, F(1, 56) = 8.70, p < .005, while base-rate primes yielded only a marginal three-way interaction with subject gender, F(1, 56) = 3.49, p < .07. Correll, Park, Judd and Wittenbrink then moved the question to a behavioural response, with a videogame in which armed and unarmed Black and white men appeared against photographic backgrounds. Forty undergraduates shot armed targets faster when the target was Black, 544 ms against 554 ms, and were slower to hold fire on unarmed Black targets, 634 ms against 623 ms, F(1, 39) = 21.86, p < .0001. What happened to that task afterwards is set out in the entry on shooter bias.

examples.text: A child is wheeled into theatre and the surgeon says they cannot operate, because the boy is their son. Listeners who hold firmly that surgeons may be of either sex still stall for a moment. Knowing what the association says and agreeing with it are separate, and the first is what stalls them.

examples.tag: The voice that answers the phone
examples.text: Somebody rings a practice, hears a woman answer and asks to be put through to the doctor, having already been put through. The category supplied the role before anything about the person did, and the caller need not believe the stereotype for it to have set the default.

examples.tag: The stereotype that can be recited and not held
examples.text: Asked what the usual picture of a group says, people who reject that picture set it out about as fully as people who endorse it. The content is cultural knowledge held in common. What separates the two is the work of overriding it once something has brought it to mind.

replication.headline: The claim that a category cue alone activates the stereotype in everyone failed the first direct test of it, and a replication in 294 subjects found the gender priming effect only where the prime and the response overlapped.
replication.detail: Lepore and Brown took Devine's Study 2 apart in 1997. Her primes carried both category labels and stereotype content, so the hostility effect could have been ordinary semantic priming. Their Study 2 primed 51 British students with thirteen category labels and neutral associates and nothing else, words such as Blacks, dreadlocks, reggae and Notting Hill. One subject was dropped for noticing the primes, leaving 25 high-prejudice and 25 low-prejudice. The three-way interaction of condition, prejudice and valence was F(1, 46) = 6.06, p < .02. High-prejudice subjects rated the target more negatively when primed, 6.76 against 5.88, t(46) = 3.43, p < .005, and less positively, 6.31 against 6.88, t(46) = 2.22, p < .025. Low-prejudice subjects moved the other way on the positive scales, 6.98 against 6.54, t(46) = 1.69, p < .05, with no difference on the negative ones. The authors call them less affected by category activation altogether, and describe the shift as a tendency in the opposite direction. Study 3 put six negative stereotype words back into the thirteen primes and ran 45 subjects, one of whom was dropped for a missing prejudice score. Both groups then rated the target more negatively when primed, 6.33 against 5.70, t(40) = 2.86, p < .005, and the three-way interaction fell to F(1, 40) = 0.04, p < .84. The simple effect still reached significance for high-prejudice subjects, t(40) = 2.62, p < .01, and not for low-prejudice ones, t(40) = 1.30, p < .1, which the authors read as endorsement having made the negative traits more accessible. Devine's result reproduces when the prime carries the stereotype and not when it carries only the category. The same two authors returned to the question in 2002 with two experiments that primed the category by lexical decision. Their abstract reports the 1997 divergence again in 57 subjects, and a reversal of it in those who noticed the link between the priming task and the impression task. Müller and Rothermund replicated the gender work in the 2014 replication issue of Social Psychology. They recruited 300 subjects and analysed 294, mean age 23.84 with a standard deviation of 5.9, after six failed to finish. Their power calculation was built on the smallest effect in the originals, Banaji and Hardin's F(1, 56) = 4.63, and called for 135 subjects per experiment at 1 minus beta of .95. Every subject did both tasks. In the gender categorisation task, where prime and response overlap, congruent primes gave 551 ms against 564 ms for incongruent, F(1, 293) = 75.54, partial eta squared 0.20. In the semantic task, where the targets were first names and city names and the judgement ignored gender, there was nothing: F(1, 293) = 1.03, p = .31, partial eta squared 0.003. The interaction with task type was F(1, 293) = 25.74, partial eta squared 0.08. Their conclusion was that automatic stereotype activation is restricted to specific conditions rather than global. Kidder, White, Hinojos, Sandoval and Crites pooled the paradigm in 2018. Their abstract gives 39 studies, 87 effect sizes and 5,497 participants, and reports that stereotype priming is moderated by the presence of prime-response relations, by participant task, by stereotype dimension, by target stimulus type, by stimulus onset asynchrony and by prime repetition. That is the moderator Müller and Rothermund's two tasks isolate, arrived at from a different direction.

study.cite: Müller, F., & Rothermund, K. (2014). What does it take to activate stereotypes? Simple primes don't seem enough. Social Psychology, 45(3), 187-193.

limits: Field experiments establish that discrimination happens. They measure what employers do, not the contents of anyone's mind. Bertrand and Mullainathan sent 4,870 fictitious resumes to over 1,300 help-wanted advertisements in Boston and Chicago, randomly assigning names that sound white or African American. White names drew callbacks 9.65% of the time and African American names 6.45%, a gap of 3.20 percentage points and a ratio of 1.50. Improving a resume helped only one group: white callbacks rose from 8.50% to 10.79% while African American callbacks moved from 6.19% to 6.70%. Employers advertising themselves as equal opportunity employers, federal contractors and larger employers did no better. The authors weigh taste-based discrimination, two families of statistical discrimination and a lexicographic search heuristic under which a recruiter stops reading at the name. Implicit stereotyping is not among the mechanisms they consider, and their design cannot separate these accounts. Quillian, Pager, Hexel and Midtbøen pooled every available American field experiment of hiring discrimination against African Americans or Latinos, 28 studies covering 55,842 applications to 26,326 positions. They focus on the 24 studies since 1989. White applicants received on average 36% more callbacks than African Americans and 24% more than Latinos, with no change over 25 years for African Americans and modest evidence of a decline for Latinos. Accounting for applicant education, applicant gender, study method, occupational groups and local labour market conditions did little to the result. Rooth's is the study usually cited to connect a measure of automatic association to real hiring. He measured callbacks for Arab-Muslim and Swedish names in a Swedish correspondence test, then gave the Implicit Association Test to the recruiters involved. The published abstract reports that the probability of inviting an Arab-Muslim applicant falls by five percentage points for a recruiter holding a one standard deviation stronger negative implicit association. The 2007 discussion paper behind it appeared under a different title, prints no such figure in its abstract, and places the association with implicit performance stereotypes rather than with implicit attitudes. That is one study, correlational at the recruiter level, and it is doing a great deal of work in arguments that cite it.
misreadings: The commonest error is the slide from discrimination to its cause. Audit studies establish that identical applications are treated differently by name, which is a fact about employers rather than a fact about the contents of their minds. Devine's own paper is misquoted in the direction of universality. The famous claim is that the stereotype fires equally in everyone. It rests on Study 2, whose primes carried both the category and its content. When Lepore and Brown removed the content, the difference between high- and low-prejudice subjects returned. What generalises from Devine is Study 1, where the two groups listed the same stereotype and no judge could tell them apart. A second error is to read any priming effect as stereotype activation. Where the prime and the correct response share a dimension, as when gendered words precede a male-or-female judgement, faster responses can come from the response rather than from the concept. Müller and Rothermund found the effect in that design and not in the design that rules the shortcut out, and Kidder and colleagues report prime-response relations as a moderator across 39 studies. Correll's Study 3 is read backwards in the same spirit. Shooter bias correlated at r = .37 with a measure of what the culture is thought to believe and at r = .38 with contact with African Americans, both p < .01. The Modern Racism Scale gave .15 and personal endorsement of the violent stereotype gave .05, neither reliable. Knowing the stereotype predicted the bias and believing it did not, which is Devine's distinction rather than a finding about prejudiced people. Finally, implicit stereotype and implicit attitude are treated as one thing. A stereotype is a belief about what a group is like and an attitude is a like or a dislike, and the tasks that measure them come apart.
